benchmark_name: Expresso-AI: Explainable Video-Based Deep Learning Models for Depression Diagnosis
authors: Felipe Moreno; Sharifa Alghowinem; Hae Won Park; Cynthia Breazeal
journal_venue: Published — 2023 11th International Conference on Affective Computing and Intelligent Interaction (ACII)
ground_truth_source: Beck Depression Inventory-II (BDI-II) scores from AVEC 2014 dataset (150 participants, 300 video recordings)
what_assessed_skills: Automatic depression severity prediction from facial videos; explainability/interpretability of deep video models via saliency maps, temporal attributions, region-wise attributions, and action unit cross-correlation
tasks_assessed: Depression severity regression from facial video clips; video-based saliency map generation; temporal attribution analysis; region-wise facial attribution analysis; action unit cross-correlation analysis
population_represented: 150 participants performing reading-aloud and freeform speech tasks (AVEC 2014); general adult population, no specific demographic breakdown reported
evaluation_method: Automated evaluation; models fine-tuned on AVEC 2014 facial video clips and evaluated on test set using Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) against BDI-II ground truth scores; interpretability assessed via DeepLift attribution maps, Kendall Tau correlation with Action Units, and region-wise relevance pooling
llms_evaluated: None — paper evaluates deep convolutional video models (R3D, R(2+1)D, Wide ResNet), not LLMs
performance_scores: Best model R(2+1)D (Kinetics-700 + MiT, depth 50): MAE=6.626, RMSE=8.543; previous benchmark DepressNet-Full: MAE=6.60, RMSE=8.88
short_summary: This paper presents Expresso-AI, a framework for explainable automatic depression diagnosis (ADD) from facial videos using deep convolutional neural networks. The authors fine-tune ResNet-based 3D video architectures (R3D, R(2+1)D, Wide ResNet) pre-trained on large action recognition datasets on the AVEC 2014 depression dataset. The framework uses the DeepLift algorithm to generate attribution maps, enabling temporal, spatial, and region-wise interpretability of model decisions. Performance is evaluated via MAE and RMSE against BDI-II scores (Automated). The best model (R(2+1)D, Kinetics-700+MiT) achieves MAE=6.626 and RMSE=8.543, outperforming prior single-face benchmarks, and qualitative/quantitative analysis reveals correlations between specific facial action units (e.g., AU9, AU4) and depression severity levels.

benchmark_name: One Year Later… The Harms Persist, But So Do We!
authors: Annika M. Schoene; Cansu Canca; Gautham Vijay Kumar; Anson Antony
institutions: Northeastern University, Boston, MA, USA; Florida International University, Miami, FL, USA
ground_truth_source: Nine-dimension behavioral scoring rubric derived empirically from output transcripts; scored by Llama 3.3 70B Instruct (automated LLM judge) and verified in full by an independent human reviewer
size_of_benchmark: 16 DSM-5 clinical conditions × 4 attack variants × 8 models × 3 repetitions per cell; prompt scripts of 9–11 turns each
what_assessed_skills: Safety safeguard robustness against adversarial multi-turn jailbreak attacks across mental health conditions; harmful content production (instructive harm); crisis resource provision; framing effects on safety calibration
tasks_assessed: Multi-turn adversarial jailbreaking (explicit harmful intent); multi-turn adversarial jailbreaking (hidden intent); intent-skipping journalism-frame attack; persistent fiction-wrapper attack with embedded minor persona; harm scoring on 9 behavioral dimensions (D1–D9)
population_represented: General population / vulnerable individuals seeking mental health information; minors mentioned as embedded persona in attack variant 2b
evaluation_method: Both (Automated + Human). LLM-as-judge: Llama 3.3 70B Instruct scored each transcript against a 9-dimension binary behavioral rubric per (model, script, run) cell; all transcripts verified in full by an independent human reviewer. Metrics: per-condition failure rate (%), harm dimension count (D1–D5 scoring, D6–D7 framing, D8–D9 mitigation), time-to-first-harmful-content (turn number).
llms_evaluated: GPT-4o; GPT-5; Gemini 2.0 Flash; Gemini 2.5 Pro; Claude Opus 4.7 (opus-4.7); Claude Sonnet 4.6 (sonnet-4.6); Grok-4.3 (xAI); DeepSeek-V4-Pro
mental_health_conditions: Suicide; Self-harm; Eating disorders; Substance use disorder (SUD); Major depressive disorder — anti-medication; Major depressive disorder — anti-therapy; Major depressive disorder — isolation; Prenatal depression; Postpartum depression; Gambling disorder; Bipolar and related disorders; Anxiety disorders; ADHD; Body-focused repetitive behaviors (BFRBs); Insomnia and sleep disorders; PTSD
performance_scores: Overall Exp 1a failure rate: 64.8%; Exp 1b: 80.5%; Exp 2a: 78.9%; Exp 2b: 67.5%. Suicide: 0% failure (all variants except 2a: 50%). MDD anti-therapy: 100% failure (Exp 1a). ADHD, MDD anti-medication, MDD isolation, gambling disorder, BFRBs, insomnia: 100% under Exp 1b. Highest-failing model (Exp 1a): GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Flash at 93.8%. Lowest-failing model (Exp 2b): Claude Sonnet 4.6 at 6.7%.
short_summary: This study evaluates the safety safeguards of eight proprietary general-purpose LLMs across 16 DSM-5 mental health conditions using four adversarial multi-turn attack variants (explicit intent, hidden intent, intent-skipping journalism frame, persistent fiction wrapper). It introduces an eight-type harm taxonomy specific to mental health LLM deployment and a nine-dimension behavioral scoring rubric to assess content harm severity. Transcripts were scored automatically by Llama 3.3 70B Instruct and fully verified by a human reviewer. Results show that reliable safeguards exist only for suicide (0% failure under Series 1), while conditions such as MDD anti-therapy, ADHD, BFRBs, insomnia, and gambling disorder reach 100% failure rates under hidden-intent attacks. The authors argue that current LLMs pose serious risks to vulnerable populations and call for clinically grounded, systematic harm categorization and safeguard implementation.

benchmark_name: PsyBridge: A Hybrid Intelligent Framework for Multi-Dimensional Mental Health Assessment and Decision Support
authors: Sunil Wanjari; Manish Thakre; Aayushi Jayant Asole; Sharwari Raut; Kwabena Adu-Duodu; Yinhao Li; Stanly Wilson
institutions: St. Vincent Pallotti College of Engineering and Technology, Nagpur, India; Government Medical College (GMC), Chandrapur, India; Newcastle University, UK
ground_truth_source: Ground truth labels assigned according to clinically established PHQ-9 and GAD-7 severity thresholds; moderate-to-severe outcomes mapped to elevated risk categories
what_assessed_skills: Multi-dimensional mental health risk classification; integration of clinical screening (PHQ-9, GAD-7), cognitive assessment (Digit Span), and personality profiling (MBTI); interpretable weighted decision-making
tasks_assessed: Mental health risk classification (Low/Moderate/High); depression severity assessment (PHQ-9); anxiety severity assessment (GAD-7); cognitive assessment; personality profiling
population_represented: Simulated patient profiles representing varying mental health severity levels (low, moderate, high risk)
evaluation_method: Automated evaluation using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score on a semi-synthetic dataset; confusion matrix analysis; ablation study; sensitivity analysis. No LLMs were directly evaluated — the system is a rule-based/weighted hybrid framework, not an LLM benchmark.
performance_scores: PsyBridge accuracy: 0.84, F1-score: 0.81; PHQ-9 only: accuracy 0.72, F1 0.69; GAD-7 only: accuracy 0.70; Clinical+Cognitive: accuracy 0.80, F1 0.78
short_summary: PsyBridge is a hybrid intelligent decision-support framework for multi-dimensional mental health assessment that integrates PHQ-9, GAD-7, cognitive (Digit Span), and personality (MBTI) modules via a weighted aggregation mechanism. It was motivated by the limitation of single-domain screening tools that miss broader cognitive and behavioural context. The framework was evaluated on a semi-synthetic dataset of 500 patient profiles using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score metrics, with ablation and sensitivity analyses also conducted. No LLMs are directly benchmarked; the paper references LLMs only in the literature review. PsyBridge achieves 0.84 accuracy and 0.81 F1-score, outperforming standalone PHQ-9 (0.72) and GAD-7 (0.70) baselines.
